title: Skew-adjoint generators and unitary flows
subtitle: G2 lecture 040000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: A real skew-symmetric two-by-two matrix K with first row zero, negative one and second row one, zero generates rotations.
body: Its exponential at time t is the rotation matrix through angle t. The identity follows from the power series, because K squared is negative identity. Suppose we are given a motion that preserves lengths and angles at every moment. What must its instantaneous generator look like? And if we start with a generator of that kind, can we prove that the motion preserves geometry for all time?

slides.title: Begin with an observable quantity
slides.lead: Imagine a vector moving through a real Euclidean space.
body: Its position at time t is called x of t. A length-preserving motion should keep the square of the vector's length constant. Why square the length? Because it is an inner product of the vector with itself, and differentiating an inner product is straightforward. Suppose the velocity is given by a linear rule: the derivative of x equals K applied to x, for some fixed matrix K. Differentiate the square of the length. The product rule gives two terms: the inner product of K x with x, and the inner product of x with K x. Use the adjoint in the first term to move K to the other side.

slides.title: A concrete two-dimensional calculation
slides.lead: Take the operator J that sends a vector with coordinates x and y to negative y and x.
body: Its matrix has zero diagonal entries, negative one in the top-right corner, and positive one in the bottom-left. Because its transpose is negative J, it is skew-symmetric. The differential equation says that the horizontal velocity is negative the vertical coordinate, and the vertical velocity is the horizontal coordinate. If the moving vector begins at one and zero, we can guess that the solution is cosine t and sine t. Differentiate those coordinates. The derivatives are negative sine t and cosine t, exactly what J prescribes. The trajectory is a unit circle.

slides.title: From one vector to an operator-valued flow
slides.lead: Instead of following one starting vector, package all solutions into a single operator Q of t.
body: For each starting vector x, Q of t sends x to its position at time t. The differential equation for Q is: its derivative equals K times Q, and Q at time zero is the identity. The matrix exponential supplies a solution: by its power-series definition, the derivative of the exponential of t K is K times that exponential. Q of t is the exponential of t K. Differentiating its power series gives the required differential equation, and plugging in zero gives the identity. To prove Q is length-preserving, we have two routes. The first applies our derivative-of-length calculation to every starting vector.

slides.title: Can we reverse the argument?
slides.lead: Suppose now that we start with a differentiable family of unitary operators Q of t.
body: It begins at the identity, and it satisfies the flow law: doing the motion for time s, then time t, is equivalent to doing it once for time s plus t. Call the derivative at time zero K. Because Q adjoint Q is always the identity, differentiating at zero gives K adjoint plus K equals zero. So K must be skew-adjoint. This is not a coincidence limited to rotations in the plane. Every differentiable unitary one-parameter group in a finite-dimensional space has a skew-adjoint infinitesimal generator. The group law also tells us the derivative at any other time: it is K times Q of t.

slides.title: What changes in three dimensions?
slides.lead: In the plane, every rotation around the origin is determined by one angle.
body: In three dimensions, we can rotate around different axes. Imagine first rotating a cube about the vertical axis, then rotating it about a horizontal axis. Reverse the order and its final orientation generally changes. That is a failure of commutativity. The two infinitesimal generators need not commute either. Consequently, the exponential of t times K one plus K two need not equal the product of the two separate exponentials. If the generator varies with time, there is a related warning.

slides.title: The complex viewpoint
slides.lead: Over a complex Hilbert space, there is another convenient description.
body: Start with a self-adjoint operator H. Multiply it by the imaginary unit and a minus sign. That gives a skew-adjoint generator. The resulting unitary flow is the exponential of negative imaginary t H. If x evolves by this flow, its squared norm remains constant. This is the operator structure behind the time-evolution equation in quantum mechanics. We do not need quantum mechanics to prove the statement. The proof rests on the identity between a self-adjoint operator and the negative adjoint of its imaginary multiple. The spectrum of H also gives a way to read the motion.

slides.title: A reconstruction challenge
slides.lead: Let us collect the reasoning without relying on a memorized theorem.
body: Start with the equation saying velocity equals K applied to position. Differentiate the squared length and rewrite the result using the adjoint. That tells you exactly why K adjoint equals negative K makes length constant. Next, construct the full flow as the exponential of t K. Show that its adjoint is its inverse. That proves the motion is unitary, not merely an isometric embedding. Finally, run the reasoning backward. Differentiate Q adjoint Q equals the identity at time zero. You will recover the skew-adjoint generator.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: For example, a rotation between spectral subspaces can be described by an exponential generator, making the continuous path of length-preserving transformations explicit.
